question: Does attention enable the required source-dependent next-token behavior?
change: Change only the DrugA/DrugB source character while holding the supplied output prefix and query position fixed.
observation: The embedding baseline has exactly unchanged candidate probabilities. The primary seed-42 single-head, multi-head and full checkpoints do not choose the correct A/B pair. The separate four-note pilot chooses A and B correctly, with expected-token probabilities 0.9987 and 0.9975, and freely generates the correct paired short notes.
verdict: Main benchmark behavior is not established by this probe; the small-grammar pilot supports the mechanism under its limited conditions.
interpretation: An attention architecture provides access to context, but a particular trained checkpoint must demonstrate useful context use. The pilot is a valid learning demonstration, not evidence of broad task transfer.
limitations: Two authored source variants; supplied prefixes are conditional probes. Main and pilot models differ in width and training data. No universal role is assigned to a head.

question: Do four bare heads improve behavior over one bare head?
change: Same model width, parameter count, bare attention policy and 1,000-update budget; change one head to four.
observation: Version 1, seeds 42/7/123: single-head recall is 0/22 for every seed; four-head recall is 4/22, 6/22 and 2/22. Both bare models produce 0/12 exact notes and 0/25 correct clinical fields at all three seeds. Mean multi-head recall is 18.2%, with observed range 9.1%-27.3%.
verdict: Consistent recall improvement in the three tested training seeds; no complete-note or clinical-preservation successes for either bare model on these diagnostics.
interpretation: Multiple bare heads improve one measured capability in this fixed-width/budget study. The outputs remain inadequate for the complete transformation. Three seeds do not prove a universal architectural advantage.
limitations: Three training seeds (initialization and minibatch order) share the same 12 selected validation notes; this is not three independent datasets. Different selected updates; no component-specific hyperparameter tuning. Version-1 flat-field grammar only; final partitions are separate descriptive evidence.

question: Does a second full decoder block improve held-out output quality?
change: One versus two pre-LN blocks, with parameter count increasing from 88,685 to 130,413.
observation: Seed 42: validation loss 1.422 versus 1.416, token accuracy 59.3% versus 63.9%, exact notes 1/12 versus 1/12, correct clinical fields 2/25 versus 1/25. Redaction recall is 11/22 for both.
verdict: Mixed; a second block does not uniformly improve generated-note metrics here.
interpretation: A small loss improvement and greater capacity do not guarantee better complete transformations. Report the capacity and quality trade-offs together.
limitations: One seed for the depth comparison; small validation generation subset; final partitions are reviewed separately.

question: Does LayerNorm help optimization or quality under these settings?
change: Full model versus removing all block and final normalization.
observation: Selected validation loss is 1.416 with normalization versus 1.431 without it. Both have 1/12 exact notes and 1/25 correct clinical fields. Maximum logged pre-clipping gradient norm is approximately 0.833 versus 2.419; final validation loss is approximately 1.798 versus 3.425. Neither run failed numerically.
verdict: Some support for scale/optimization differences; generated-quality evidence is mixed and preliminary.
interpretation: The recorded traces support a setup-specific stability/scale benefit, not a claim that normalization was required for any learning or that every output metric improved.
limitations: Gradient maxima cover logged validation intervals, not every update. One seed; normalization removal changes parameters; learning rate was not separately tuned per variant.

question: Do residual paths improve learning and output quality here?
change: Full model versus omitting residual additions while retaining the other declared components.
observation: The full model has lower selected validation loss, 1.416 versus 1.586. The no-residual model has more exact diagnostic notes, 3/12 versus 1/12, more correct redactions, 16/22 versus 11/22, and more preserved clinical fields, 7/25 versus 1/25.
verdict: Mixed; the generated-quality direction contradicts a blanket residual-benefit claim under this budget.
interpretation: Different objectives rank the variants differently. The evidence should be shown rather than rewritten to match the architectural expectation.
limitations: One seed and 12 diagnostics; different selected updates; no architecture-specific optimizer tuning. This is not a universal conclusion against residuals.

question: Does the FFN improve the transformation?
change: Full model versus omitting both FFN update branches and their unused pre-normalization parameters.
observation: The full model improves selected validation loss, 1.416 versus 1.578, and redaction recall, 11/22 versus 8/22. No-FFN has 2/12 exact notes versus 1/12 and 2/25 preserved clinical fields versus 1/25.
interpretation: The FFN helps some criteria in this run, but the complete-note metrics do not move uniformly. The architectural and parameter changes must be disclosed.
limitations: One seed; small diagnostic subset; coupled branch/normalization removal and parameter-count difference.

question: Do individual heads make different contributions?
change: Zero one head's context before output projection, then test two validation-selected pairs without retraining.
observation: At full-model update 400, baseline recall is 7/15. Disabling L0 H1 gives 0/15; L0 H0 gives 4/15. L1 H0 leaves free outputs unchanged on these eight notes, yet conditional loss rises from 0.624 to 0.698. The selected L1 pair gives 2/15 recall.
verdict: Supported as different measured dependencies of this checkpoint; semantic specialization remains unestablished.
interpretation: Importance depends on the metric and intervention. No visible free-output change does not imply no probability-level contribution. A harmful change identifies dependence, not a permanent clinical role.
limitations: Only eight notes; baseline MRN recall is already zero and several categories have one example. Pair selection uses these validation diagnostics and is exploratory. Head indices do not identify equivalent functions across seeds.

question: Does redaction transfer to new entities and layouts?
change: Evaluate all four complete 50-note final partitions after freezing and reviewing the seed-42 protocol.
observation: All32 version-1 architecture/partition rows completed. Full model, seed42 selected update400: known names/known layouts gives 7/50 exact notes,76/113 correct identifier replacements and7/93 clinical fields; known/new gives0/50,34/124 and4/88; new/known gives0/50,24/103 and1/107; new/new gives0/50,22/136 and1/82. No exact-surface leakage was detected, despite poor note/content quality.
verdict: Broad transfer is not supported. The measured full-model outputs degrade in novel conditions and remain weak even in the familiar condition.
interpretation: Redaction markers, absence of exact-surface leakage and valid EOS do not establish a useful preserved note. Separate names/layout conditions and complete-note/clinical counts reveal failures hidden by a single metric. These frozen models were not tuned from final outcomes.
limitations: One selected checkpoint/seed for final partitions. Different50-note samples and field supports; these are descriptive conditions, not matched source pairs. Synthetic flat-field grammar, shared control layouts, recurring dates and exact-surface leakage limits. The corrected assignment-format series is a separate development study.

question: Does sampling temperature change output reliability?
change: Sample at 0.1, 0.7 and 1.2 using the same update-400 checkpoint, eight notes and declared seeds.
observation: Correct redactions are 7/15, 7/15 and 0/15; exact notes are 1/8, 0/8 and 0/8; valid EOS terminations are 8/8, 8/8 and 6/8, respectively.
verdict: Supported as an observed difference in these trials, with substantial uncertainty.
interpretation: Higher temperature spread probability and produced worse measured behavior in this small sample. Low positive temperature is still sampling, not a guarantee of correctness or deterministic decoding.
limitations: One sampling seed per note at each temperature; eight prompts; weak selected checkpoint. These trials do not estimate a general temperature-quality relationship.
